extracted.intended_audience: postcard collectors, vintage-humor enthusiasts, and general readers interested in Punch and historical jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing what makes early 20th-century 'Good Jokes from PUNCH' postcards funny (or not), with attention to cultural, visual, temporal, and performance factors that affect humor reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence / not funny out of context
rubrics_metrics.description: “these jokes are not funny when read (or heard) out of context.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses that many of the Tuck postcards rely on surrounding information (visuals, cultural knowledge, situational setup) to land; removing that context (e.g., reading only the caption) often destroys the joke. Anti-pattern: presenting isolated captions without images or explanatory notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge as a characteristic of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: “One characteristic of humor is knowledge! Without understanding the circumstance of a joke why would it be funny?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience familiarity with reference points (e.g., knowing what 'Bradshaw’s' refers to) is essential for understanding and enjoying many jokes. Example: the featured cab-price gag depends on knowing historical price terminology and Bradshaw's as a reference source. Scoring note: jokes that require obscure knowledge should be judged on whether the intended audience likely has that knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal (visual + text) integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Many postcards pair illustration and caption; the absurdity and humour are recognized by seeing the image alongside the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that illustrations by well-known artists supply essential situational cues. Evaluate whether the image clarifies or amplifies the caption. Anti-pattern: relying solely on text when the original humor depended on visual detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and telling / performer skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke's funniness can depend on who tells it and how: e.g., the M*A*S*H anecdote — Hawkeye's telling failed but B. J.'s telling made everyone 'keel over laughing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing, cadence, emphasis, and the teller's skill when judging a joke's success. Scoring note: identical wording can score differently depending on delivery; written transcriptions may lose this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/style differences (subtle vs in-your-face)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the British have a very subtle sense of humor, whereas we Americans prefer a more 'in your face' approach to a good laugh.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cultural style preferences: subtle irony, understatement, and dry wit (British) vs broader, louder cues (American). A joke should be evaluated relative to the stylistic norms of its originating audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal / generational comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: If readers from a different generation knew what 'Bradshaw’s' was, this joke may well be fall-down hilarious!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor using archaic or era-specific referents may fail for modern readers. When assessing vintage jokes, note whether time-sensitive references are explained or assumed; judge on intent and target-era audience rather than modern ubiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity and recognizability of the situation
rubrics_metrics.description: The example of the woman arguing a cab price in the rain shows that recognizing the absurd situation is key to finding it funny: 'It takes little imagination to recognize the absurdity...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the situation is presented clearly enough for readers to perceive the absurdity. If the absurd element is obscure or poorly signaled, the joke weakens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline presence / clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied by the article's title 'Do They Have a Punch?' and the pasted examples: jokes rely on a concise turn or twist (the punch) to score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the joke culminates in a clear punchline or twist and whether that punchline is accessible given the context and delivery. Anti-pattern: meandering setups with no clear payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay and double-meaning exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like the 'light of his life' → 'the light was always going out' show reliance on metaphorical/ambiguous phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge effectiveness of puns and double-meanings: is the ambiguity clever and discoverable by the intended audience, or forced and confusing? Examples in the article illustrate successful brief wordplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting / market localization
rubrics_metrics.description: “It should come as no surprise that these cards were marketed only in Great Britain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a joke was designed for a specific geographic or cultural market; successful jokes align with the target market's knowledge and tastes. Marketing decisions (e.g., selling only in Great Britain) often reflect that alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived intelligence of the joke (not merely 'bad' but 'dumb')
rubrics_metrics.description: The author: 'Someone, other than I, should say there are no bad jokes, just dumb ones or stupid ones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between jokes that fail due to contextual/mis-delivery reasons and those that are simply weak in conception. Evaluate whether failure stems from execution/context or from inherent lack of wit.
